claim: Rhodotorula/Rhodosporidium species are widely distributed in the phyllosphere and diverse soils.
source: Rhodotorula/Rhodosporidium species are widely distributed in the phyllosphere and diverse soils (Rosa and Peter, 2006; Sláviková et al., 2009; Butinar et al., 2005; Pulschen et al., 2015).
evidence: Multiple citations support this claim about the distribution of these species.

claim: Rhodosporidium toruloides accumulates high concentrations of carotenoid pigments.
source: They accumulate high concentrations of carotenoid pigments (Mata-Gómez et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014), giving their colonies a distinctive orange, red, or pink hue.
evidence: Citations support the claim about carotenoid accumulation.

claim: Carotenoid pigments give Rhodosporidium toruloides colonies a distinctive orange, red, or pink hue.
source: They accumulate high concentrations of carotenoid pigments (Mata-Gómez et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014), giving their colonies a distinctive orange, red, or pink hue.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the visual appearance of colonies.

claim: R. toruloides can accumulate as much as 70% of cellular biomass as lipids under nitrogen limitation.
source: When R. toruloides is cultured under nitrogen (Zhu et al., 2012), sulfur (Wu et al., 2011), or phosphorus (Wu et al., 2010) limitation, it can accumulate as much as 70% of cellular biomass as lipids (Wiebe et al., 2012), primarily as triacylglycerides (TAG).
evidence: Citation to Wiebe et al., 2012 supports this quantitative claim.

claim: R. toruloides can accumulate as much as 70% of cellular biomass as lipids under sulfur limitation.
source: When R. toruloides is cultured under nitrogen (Zhu et al., 2012), sulfur (Wu et al., 2011), or phosphorus (Wu et al., 2010) limitation, it can accumulate as much as 70% of cellular biomass as lipids (Wiebe et al., 2012), primarily as triacylglycerides (TAG).
evidence: Citation to Wu et al., 2011 and Wiebe et al., 2012 support this claim.

claim: R. toruloides can accumulate as much as 70% of cellular biomass as lipids under phosphorus limitation.
source: When R. toruloides is cultured under nitrogen (Zhu et al., 2012), sulfur (Wu et al., 2011), or phosphorus (Wu et al., 2010) limitation, it can accumulate as much as 70% of cellular biomass as lipids (Wiebe et al., 2012), primarily as triacylglycerides (TAG).
evidence: Citation to Wu et al., 2010 and Wiebe et al., 2012 support this claim.

claim: Lipids accumulated by R. toruloides under nutrient limitation are primarily triacylglycerides (TAG).
source: When R. toruloides is cultured under nitrogen (Zhu et al., 2012), sulfur (Wu et al., 2011), or phosphorus (Wu et al., 2010) limitation, it can accumulate as much as 70% of cellular biomass as lipids (Wiebe et al., 2012), primarily as triacylglycerides (TAG).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the composition of accumulated lipids.

claim: Lipid droplets emerge from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane.
source: Lipid droplets emerge from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane as a core of TAG surrounded by sterol esters, a phospholipid monolayer derived from ER phospholipids, and a targeted ensemble of proteins mediating inter-organelle interaction, protein trafficking, cellular lipid trafficking and regulated carbon flux in and out of the lipid droplet (Walther and Farese, 2012; Farese and Walther, 2009; Gao and Goodman, 2015).
evidence: Citations support this claim about lipid droplet biogenesis.

claim: Lipid droplets consist of a core of TAG surrounded by sterol esters, a phospholipid monolayer, and proteins.
source: Lipid droplets emerge from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane as a core of TAG surrounded by sterol esters, a phospholipid monolayer derived from ER phospholipids, and a targeted ensemble of proteins mediating inter-organelle interaction, protein trafficking, cellular lipid trafficking and regulated carbon flux in and out of the lipid droplet (Walther and Farese, 2012; Farese and Walther, 2009; Gao and Goodman, 2015).
evidence: Citations support this structural description of lipid droplets.

claim: Aberrant lipid droplet formation contributes to many human diseases.
source: Aberrant lipid droplet formation contributes to many human diseases (Krahmer et al., 2013a; Welte, 2015) and impacts cellular processes as diverse as autophagy (Shpilka et al., 2015) and mitosis (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Citations support this claim about the role of lipid droplets in disease.

claim: Lipid droplet formation impacts autophagy.
source: Aberrant lipid droplet formation contributes to many human diseases (Krahmer et al., 2013a; Welte, 2015) and impacts cellular processes as diverse as autophagy (Shpilka et al., 2015) and mitosis (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to Shpilka et al., 2015 supports this claim.

claim: Lipid droplet formation impacts mitosis.
source: Aberrant lipid droplet formation contributes to many human diseases (Krahmer et al., 2013a; Welte, 2015) and impacts cellular processes as diverse as autophagy (Shpilka et al., 2015) and mitosis (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to Yang et al., 2016 supports this claim.

claim: R. toruloides forms large lipid droplets under a variety of conditions.
source: The propensity of R. toruloides to form large lipid droplets under a variety of conditions makes it an attractive platform to study conserved aspects of the cellular biology of these important organelles across diverse eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about R. toruloides' lipid droplet formation.

claim: Wild isolates of R. toruloides can produce lipids and carotenoids from glucose.
source: Wild isolates of R. toruloides can produce lipids and carotenoids from a wide variety of carbon sources including glucose (Wiebe et al., 2012), xylose (Wiebe et al., 2012), and acetate (Huang et al., 2016), as well as complex biomass hydrolysates (Fei et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to Wiebe et al., 2012 supports this claim.

claim: Wild isolates of R. toruloides can produce lipids and carotenoids from xylose.
source: Wild isolates of R. toruloides can produce lipids and carotenoids from a wide variety of carbon sources including glucose (Wiebe et al., 2012), xylose (Wiebe et al., 2012), and acetate (Huang et al., 2016), as well as complex biomass hydrolysates (Fei et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to Wiebe et al., 2012 supports this claim.

claim: Wild isolates of R. toruloides can produce lipids and carotenoids from acetate.

evidence: Citation to Huang et al., 2016 supports this claim.

claim: Wild isolates of R. toruloides can produce lipids and carotenoids from complex biomass hydrolysates.

evidence: Citation to Fei et al., 2016 supports this claim.

claim: R. toruloides is relatively tolerant to osmotic stress.
source: They are relatively tolerant to many forms of stress including osmotic stress (Singh et al., 2016) and growth-inhibiting compounds in biomass hydrolysates (Hu et al., 2009; Kitahara et al., 2014).

claim: R. toruloides is relatively tolerant to growth-inhibiting compounds in biomass hydrolysates.

claim: R. toruloides has been engineered to produce fatty alcohols.
source: Rhodosporidium toruloides has been engineered to produce lipid-derived bioproducts such as fatty alcohols (Fillet et al., 2015) and erucic acid (Fillet et al., 2017) from synthetic pathways.
evidence: Citation to Fillet et al., 2015 supports this claim.

claim: R. toruloides has been engineered to produce erucic acid.
source: Rhodosporidium toruloides has been engineered to produce lipid-derived bioproducts such as fatty alcohols (Fillet et al., 2015) and erucic acid (Fillet et al., 2017) from synthetic pathways.

claim: R. toruloides has been engineered for enhanced carotenoid production.
source: To enable more efficient production of terpene-derived and lipid-derived chemicals, it has also been engineered for enhanced carotenoid (Lee et al., 2016) and lipid (Zhang et al., 2016a) production.
evidence: Citation to Lee et al., 2016 supports this claim.

claim: R. toruloides has been engineered for enhanced lipid production.
source: To enable more efficient production of terpene-derived and lipid-derived chemicals, it has also been engineered for enhanced carotenoid (Lee et al., 2016) and lipid (Zhang et al., 2016a) production.
evidence: Citation to Zhang et al., 2016a supports this claim.

claim: Transcriptomic and proteomic analysis of R. toruloides in nitrogen limited conditions identified over 2,000 genes with altered transcript abundance.
source: Recently, transcriptomic and proteomic analysis of R. toruloides in nitrogen limited conditions (Zhu et al., 2012) identified over 2,000 genes with altered transcript abundance and over 500 genes with altered protein abundance during lipid accumulation.
evidence: Citation to Zhu et al., 2012 supports this claim.

claim: Transcriptomic and proteomic analysis of R. toruloides in nitrogen limited conditions identified over 500 genes with altered protein abundance.
source: Recently, transcriptomic and proteomic analysis of R. toruloides in nitrogen limited conditions (Zhu et al., 2012) identified over 2,000 genes with altered transcript abundance and over 500 genes with altered protein abundance during lipid accumulation.
evidence: Citation to Zhu et al., 2012 supports this claim.

claim: Proteomics of isolated lipid droplets identified over 250 lipid droplet-associated proteins in R. toruloides.
source: Proteomics of isolated lipid droplets (Zhu et al., 2015) identified over 250 lipid droplet-associated proteins including fatty acid synthesis genes, several putative lipases, a homolog of the lipolysis-regulating protein perilipin (Bickel et al., 2009), vesicle trafficking proteins such as Rab GTPases and SNARE proteins, as well as several mitochondrial and peroxisomal proteins.
evidence: Citation to Zhu et al., 2015 supports this claim.

claim: Differential transcript or protein abundance under nitrogen limitation is suggestive of function in lipid accumulation, but transcriptional regulation and gene function are often poorly correlated in laboratory conditions.
source: Differential transcript or protein abundance under nitrogen limitation is suggestive of function in lipid accumulation, but transcriptional regulation and gene function are often poorly correlated in laboratory conditions (Price et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation to Price et al., 2013 supports this claim.

claim: Sequestration in the lipid droplet may help regulate availability of some proteins for functions not necessarily related to lipid metabolism.
source: Similarly, sequestration in the lipid droplet may help regulate availability of some proteins for functions not necessarily related to lipid metabolism (Cermelli et al., 2006).
evidence: Citation to Cermelli et al., 2006 supports this claim.

claim: The study developed a method for high-throughput genetics called RB-TDNAseq using sequence-barcoded Agrobacterium tumefaciens T-DNA insertions.
source: We developed a method for high-throughput genetics (RB-TDNAseq), using sequence-barcoded Agrobacterium tumefaciens T-DNA insertions.

claim: The study validated results with 35 targeted deletion strains.

claim: The study improved the existing genome assembly and annotation for R. toruloides IFO 0880 using long-read PacBio sequencing.
source: To enable functional genomics in R. toruloides IFO 0880, we first improved the existing genome assembly and annotation (Zhang et al., 2016a) using a combination of long-read PacBio sequencing for a more complete de novo assembly, a more comprehensive informatics approach for gene model predictions and functional annotation, and manual refinement of those models using evidence from mRNA sequencing (Genbank accession LCTV02000000), also available at the Mycocosm genome portal (Grigoriev et al., 2014) (see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: The study used a more comprehensive informatics approach for gene model predictions and functional annotation.
source: To enable functional genomics in R. toruloides IFO 0880, we first improved the existing genome assembly and annotation (Zhang et al., 2016a) using a combination of long-read PacBio sequencing for a more complete de novo assembly, a more comprehensive informatics approach for gene model predictions and functional annotation, and manual refinement of those models using evidence from mRNA sequencing (Genbank accession LCTV02000000), also available at the Mycocosm genome portal (Grigoriev et al., 2014) (see Appendix 1 for details).

claim: The study generated a diverse library of binary ATMT plasmids bearing nourseothricin resistance cassettes with ~10 million unique 20 base-pair sequence 'barcodes'.
source: In brief, we generated a diverse library of binary ATMT plasmids bearing nourseothricin resistance cassettes with ~10 million unique 20 base-pair sequence 'barcodes' by efficient Type IIS restriction enzyme cloning (Engler et al., 2008), introduced the library into A. tumefaciens EHA105 by electroporation, then transformed R. toruloides with ATMT.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: The study mapped the unique locations of 293,613 individual barcoded T-DNA insertions in the R. toruloides genome.
source: Using a TnSeq-like protocol, we mapped the unique locations of 293,613 individual barcoded T-DNA insertions in the R. toruloides genome (see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study.

claim: Insertions were sufficiently well dispersed to map at least one T-DNA in 93% of nuclear genes.
source: Insertions were sufficiently well dispersed to map at least one T-DNA in 93% of nuclear genes, despite some local and fine-scale biases in insertion rates (see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study.

claim: Insertion density in coding regions followed an approximately normal distribution centered on nine inserts per thousand base pairs.
source: Insertion density in coding regions followed an approximately normal distribution (as expected for random integration) centered on nine inserts per thousand base pairs, except for a subpopulation of genes with fewer than two inserts/kb (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study, supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Genes with very low insertion rates were highly enriched for orthologs of genes reported as essential in Aspergillus nidulans.
source: These very low-insertion genes were highly enriched for orthologs of genes reported as essential in Aspergillus nidulans (Arnaud et al., 2012), Cryptococcus neoformans (Ianiri and Idnurm, 2015), Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Cherry et al., 2012), or Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Wood et al., 2012), or for which only heterokaryons could be obtained in the Neurospora crassa deletion collection (Colot et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study, supported by citations.

claim: The study cultured the mutant pool in defined medium (DM) consisting of glucose and yeast nitrogen base without amino acids.
source: We cultured the mutant pool in defined medium (DM), consisting of glucose and yeast nitrogen base without amino acids and in DM supplemented with 'drop-out mix complete' (DOC), a mix of amino acids, adenine, uracil, p-aminobenzoic acid, and inositol.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: Mutants for 28 genes had fitness scores suggesting auxotrophy.
source: Mutants for 28 genes had fitness scores suggesting auxotrophy: fitness defects in non-supplemented media (FDM < −1) with consistently different scores in supplemented versus non-supplemented media (TDM-DOC < −3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study.

claim: When the mutant pool was grown in defined media with methionine or arginine supplementation, the 28 auxotrophic mutants partitioned into 11 mutants rescued by methionine, eight mutants rescued by arginine, seven mutants rescued by neither amino acid and two mutants rescued by both amino acids.
source: When we grew the mutant pool in defined media with methionine or arginine supplementation (Figure 2B), the 28 auxotrophic mutants partitioned into 11 mutants rescued by methionine, eight mutants rescued by arginine, seven mutants rescued by neither amino acid and two mutants rescued by both amino acids.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: All of the identified methionine and arginine auxotrophic mutants have orthologous genes for which mutants are auxotrophic for methionine/cysteine or arginine, respectively, in S. cerevisiae or A. nidulans.
source: All of the identified methionine and arginine auxotrophic mutants have orthologous genes for which mutants are auxotrophic for methionine/cysteine or arginine, respectively, in S. cerevisiae or A. nidulans.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of fitness scores for genes with F < −1 and T < −3 versus Time 0 in any supplementation condition resulted in clusters that included twelve and nine mutants rescued by methionine and arginine respectively.
source: Alternatively, when we hierarchically clustered the fitness scores for genes with F < −1 and T < −3 versus Time 0 in any supplementation condition (Figure 2C), the resulting clusters included twelve and nine mutants rescued by methionine and arginine respectively; this was a nearly complete recovery of genes with predicted functions in this pathway (shown in Figure 2D–E with additional discussion in Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study, supported by Figure 2C.

claim: The study used RB-TDNAseq to measure mutant fitness on oleic acid as the sole carbon source.
source: For this purpose, we used RB-TDNAseq to measure mutant fitness on three fatty acids as the sole carbon source: oleic acid (the most abundant fatty acid in R. toruloides [Li et al., 2007]) ricinoleic acid (a high-value fatty acid produced naturally in plants (Dyer et al., 2008) and synthetically in fungi [Holic et al., 2012]), and methyl ricinoleic acid (a ricinoleic acid derivative used in lactone production [Endrizzi et al., 1996]).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: A total of 129 genes had consistently low fitness scores on one or more fatty acids.

evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study.

claim: Mutants for mitochondrial enzymes had the most consistent fitness scores across all three fatty acids.
source: Mutants for mitochondrial enzymes had the most consistent fitness scores across all three fatty acids, whereas mutants for the peroxisomal enzymes and peroxins had more variable fitness scores among fatty acids.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study.

claim: Mutants for peroxisomal enzymes and peroxins had more variable fitness scores among fatty acids.
source: Mutants for mitochondrial enzymes had the most consistent fitness scores across all three fatty acids, whereas mutants for the peroxisomal enzymes and peroxins had more variable fitness scores among fatty acids.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study.

claim: Mutants for seven peroxisomal beta-oxidation enzymes and three peroxins had different fitness scores on oleic acid versus ricinoleic acid and methylricinoleic acid.
source: Mutants for seven peroxisomal beta-oxidation enzymes and three peroxins had different fitness scores on oleic acid versus ricinoleic acid and methylricinoleic acid (listed in Appendix 1, full fitness scores in Supplementary file 2), while 11 other predicted peroxisomal beta-oxidation enzymes had no consistent fitness scores at all.
